A virtual screen is, from the data scientist's point of view, a sorting problem with an expensive verification step. A model orders a library of molecules; the laboratory can afford to buy and test a few dozen of them; the question is whether the top of that order contains more active compounds than a random draw would, and by how much. This unit never runs a docking program and never opens a protein structure: it starts where the group's screening pipelines end, with a table of molecules and scores, and teaches the analytics of a ranked list - the metrics that measure early recognition, the confidence intervals they need, the ways a benchmark can flatter a method that has learnt nothing about pharmacology, and the arithmetic that converts an impressive enrichment factor into the sober number of compounds a student will actually have to order.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad trata el análisis estadístico del resultado de un cribado virtual: una lista ordenada de moléculas. Se construyen cuatro rankings basados en ligando (máxima similitud de Tanimoto a activos conocidos, un puntaje de k vecinos más cercanos sobre huellas moleculares, la probabilidad de un modelo QSAR reajustado aquí y una distancia en el espacio de descriptores) y se evalúan desde los primeros principios con la curva ROC y su área, los factores de enriquecimiento al 1 % y 5 %, BEDROC, RIE y la tasa de aciertos entre los primeros k, con intervalos de confianza obtenidos por bootstrap sobre activos y señuelos. Luego se desmonta el propio banco de pruebas: señuelos emparejados por propiedades frente a señuelos aleatorios, la sensibilidad al conjunto de referencia, el diagnóstico de enriquecimiento artificial (un bosque aleatorio que separa activos de señuelos usando solo propiedades fisicoquímicas) y el efecto de una prevalencia realista de 1 % y 0,1 %. Finalmente se comparan cuatro esquemas de consenso con el mejor ranking individual, se examina la correlación entre puntaje y tamaño molecular junto con la eficiencia de ligando, y se selecciona una lista de cincuenta compuestos con un criterio de diversidad defendible.

Learning objectives

  • Evaluate a screening campaign with the right metrics - ROC-AUC, enrichment factor at 1 % and 5 %, BEDROC, RIE and hit rate at k - implementing each from its definition and attaching bootstrap confidence intervals.
  • Explain decoy design (property matching, the DUD-E logic), analogue bias and artificial enrichment, and why a good area under the curve on a convenient decoy set can mean very little.
  • Combine several ranking criteria (z-score, rank-by-rank, rank-by-vote, exponential consensus) and test whether the consensus actually improves on the best single ranking.
  • Analyse a screening output table: score distributions, score-property correlations and size bias, the diversity of a hit list, and the selection of compounds for testing under a fixed budget.
  • Translate a retrospective enrichment into a prospective expectation using the base rate of actives in a real library.

1. What a virtual screen produces, and what this unit does with it

A screening campaign has three stages. A library is assembled - purchasable catalogue, in-house collection or virtual enumeration. A score is then computed for every molecule: either ligand-based, comparing the candidate with molecules already known to act on the target, or structure-based, estimating how well it fits a pocket of the protein. Finally - the only stage that costs money - a handful of top-ranked molecules are bought and assayed. The computational part therefore produces one deliverable: an ordering of the library, plus the numbers that justify trusting its top.

Everything in this unit happens after the score exists: the campaign becomes a table with a score and a ground-truth label, and we ask how to measure that the ordering is good, how uncertain that measurement is, what makes it optimistic, and what it predicts about a prospective experiment. The screening programs themselves (docking engines, pharmacophore searches, shape overlays) are taught in the bioinformatics course; their output has the same form, so the analytics transfer unchanged[34].

Domain context

A target is the protein whose activity a drug should change; this unit uses ROCK1 (Rho-associated protein kinase 1), an enzyme the group studies, as the target. A compound is called an active when a laboratory assay shows that it inhibits the target at a low concentration; potency is reported as pActivity = -log10 of the molar concentration producing the effect, so pActivity 7 means 100 nM and each unit is a factor of ten. A decoy is a molecule assumed inactive against the target, included in a benchmark so that a ranking has something to be wrong about. A fingerprint is a binary vector in which each bit records the presence of a small substructure, and the Tanimoto coefficient between two fingerprints is the number of bits they share divided by the number of bits either has - a similarity between 0 and 1. A scaffold is the ring system of a molecule once its side chains are stripped (the Bemis-Murcko framework[20]); compounds sharing a scaffold are usually analogues from the same medicinal-chemistry programme. Enrichment is the central word of the unit: how many more actives the top of a ranking contains than a random selection of the same size.

The frozen benchmark is screening_library.csv: 1,327 ROCK1 actives (curated ChEMBL measurements[23], pActivity at least 6.5), 6,923 decoys matched to them in physico-chemical property space following the DUD-E logic[2], and 3,768 decoys drawn at random from the same pool of molecules measured at eight unrelated non-kinase targets, all filtered to Tanimoto similarity below 0.35 against every known ROCK1 ligand. Two decoy sets are frozen on purpose.

The table shows the two design decisions that will drive every later result. The matched decoys look like the actives: mean molecular weight 405 against 379 Da, mean cLogP 3.41 against 3.44, mean topological polar surface area (TPSA) 80 against 85 square angstroms. The random decoys do not: their weight spreads much wider, their polarity is lower and their rotatable-bond count higher. A ranking that separates actives from random decoys may be detecting the target pharmacology, or it may be detecting that ROCK1 inhibitors are kinase-like molecules with a particular size and polarity profile - the two explanations are confounded, and only the matched set partially decouples them.

The second decision is the active fraction, 0.110 in this file. A real screening library has one active in a thousand or in ten thousand[30]. An 11 % benchmark is convenient (every metric is stable because there are many actives) and dangerous (several metrics saturate, and the base-rate arithmetic of a prospective campaign is completely different). Section 12 subsamples the actives to put that right.

2. Fingerprints and the Tanimoto coefficient, by hand and by code

A ligand-based score needs a notion of molecular similarity. The standard one in the laboratory is the Tanimoto coefficient over Morgan (extended-connectivity) fingerprints[10]: each atom environment up to a radius of two bonds is hashed into one of 2,048 bit positions, so a molecule becomes a sparse binary vector of substructure flags. For two such vectors with $a$ bits set in the first, $b$ in the second and $c$ in common,

$$T = \frac{c}{a + b - c}.$$

The denominator is the number of bits set in at least one of the two vectors, so $T = 1$ only for molecules with identical bit patterns and $T = 0$ when they share no environment at all. Values are not calibrated across fingerprint types: 0.35 is a weak resemblance for Morgan bits and a near-identity for some other fingerprints, which is why a similarity threshold must always be reported together with the fingerprint that produced it[11].

2.1 A worked example done by hand

Take two very small molecules, phenol (c1ccccc1O) and aniline (c1ccccc1N), and a fingerprint of radius 1 folded to 64 bits so that the vectors can be written out. Each molecule contributes one bit per atom environment: the six aromatic carbons with their neighbours, the substituted carbon, and the oxygen or nitrogen. By hand we expect the two molecules to share the environments of the unsubstituted aromatic carbons and to differ in the environments that include the heteroatom. If $a = 10$, $b = 10$ and $c = 6$, then

$$T = \frac{6}{10 + 10 - 6} = \frac{6}{14} = 0.4286.$$

The next cell computes the three counts from RDKit and evaluates the same fraction, so that the arithmetic above can be checked rather than believed.

g1 = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=1, fpSize=64)
fa, fb = (g1.GetFingerprint(Chem.MolFromSmiles(s)) for s in ["c1ccccc1O", "c1ccccc1N"])
a, b = fa.GetNumOnBits(), fb.GetNumOnBits()
c = len(set(fa.GetOnBits()) & set(fb.GetOnBits()))
print("bits set: phenol a =", a, "| aniline b =", b, "| shared c =", c)
print("Tanimoto by hand  : c / (a + b - c) = %d / %d = %.4f" % (c, a + b - c, c / (a + b - c)))
print("Tanimoto by RDKit : %.4f" % DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fa, fb))

bits set: phenol a = 7 | aniline b = 7 | shared c = 4
Tanimoto by hand  : c / (a + b - c) = 4 / 10 = 0.4000
Tanimoto by RDKit : 0.4000

The hand calculation and RDKit agree to the last digit, which is the point of the exercise: the similarity used in every ranking below is a ratio of two integers that a student can count, not an opaque model output. The production fingerprints used from here on have radius 2 and 2,048 bits, the setting used throughout the group's work and in the frozen library's own construction.

gen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048)
mols = [Chem.MolFromSmiles(s) for s in lib["std_smiles"]]
fps = [gen.GetFingerprint(m) for m in mols]
lab = lib["label"].to_numpy()
X = lib[PROPS].to_numpy(dtype=float)

      % (np.mean([f.GetNumOnBits() for f, l in zip(fps, lab) if l == 1]),
         np.mean([f.GetNumOnBits() for f, l in zip(fps, lab) if l == 0])))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
probe = rng.choice(np.where(lab == 1)[0], 40, replace=False)      # 40 reference actives for the picture
def max_sim(ref, targets):
    R = [fps[i] for i in ref]
    return np.array([max(DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[j], R)) for j in targets])
sims = {k: max_sim(probe, np.where(m.to_numpy() if hasattr(m, "to_numpy") else m)[0])
        for k, m in groups.items()}
for k, v in sims.items():
    print("%-15s max-Tanimoto to the 40 probes: median %.3f, 95th pct %.3f" % (k, np.median(v), np.percentile(v, 95)))

3. Four ligand-based rankings

A ranking must be computable from information available before the assay. We therefore split the library into a training part, which plays the role of what the laboratory already knows, and an evaluation part, which plays the role of the untested library. Forty per cent of the actives and forty per cent of each decoy set go to training; the remaining sixty per cent are ranked and scored. All four rankings see exactly the same training information, so the comparison between them is fair.

  1. Maximum Tanimoto similarity to any training active - the oldest and still the strongest ligand-based baseline[6].
  2. Fingerprint k-nearest-neighbour score: the mean Tanimoto to the five most similar training actives, which suppresses the influence of a single lucky analogue.
  3. QSAR probability: a random forest trained here on the twelve physico-chemical descriptors of training actives and training decoys, scoring each evaluation molecule by its predicted probability of being active.
  4. Descriptor distance: minus the Mahalanobis distance from the molecule to the training actives in standardised descriptor space - a one-class score that uses no decoy information at all.

The four differ in what they can see. The first two use substructure identity, the third uses whole-molecule properties with decoy supervision, the fourth uses whole-molecule properties without it. Keeping a deliberately weak member in the panel is useful: consensus methods in section 13 will have to cope with it.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx_groups = {"active": np.where(lab == 1)[0],
              "matched": np.where(lib["decoy_set"].to_numpy() == "property_matched")[0],
              "random": np.where(lib["decoy_set"].to_numpy() == "random")[0]}
train, test = {}, {}
for k, v in idx_groups.items():
    perm = rng.permutation(v); cut = int(0.4 * len(v))
    train[k], test[k] = perm[:cut], perm[cut:]
print({k: (len(train[k]), len(test[k])) for k in idx_groups})

tr_act = train["active"]
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X[np.concatenate([tr_act, train["matched"]])])
Xs = scaler.transform(X)

def build_rankings(eval_idx, decoy_key):
    '''The four ligand-based scores for one evaluation set; training information only.'''
    R = [fps[i] for i in tr_act]
    sorted_sims = [sorted(DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[j], R)) for j in eval_idx]
    s_max = np.array([v[-1] for v in sorted_sims])
    s_knn = np.array([np.mean(v[-5:]) for v in sorted_sims])
    tri = np.concatenate([tr_act, train[decoy_key]])
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X[tri], lab[tri])
    s_qsar = rf.predict_proba(X[eval_idx])[:, 1]
    mu = Xs[tr_act].mean(axis=0)
    P = np.linalg.inv(np.cov(Xs[tr_act].T) + 1e-6 * np.eye(len(PROPS)))
    d = Xs[eval_idx] - mu
    s_dist = -np.sqrt(np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", d, P, d))
    return pd.DataFrame({"max_tanimoto": s_max, "knn5": s_knn, "qsar_rf": s_qsar, "desc_dist": s_dist},
                        index=eval_idx)

ev_m = np.concatenate([test["active"], test["matched"]])
ev_r = np.concatenate([test["active"], test["random"]])
S_m, S_r = build_rankings(ev_m, "matched"), build_rankings(ev_r, "random")
y_m, y_r = lab[ev_m], lab[ev_r]
print("evaluation set (matched decoys): %d molecules, %d actives, prevalence %.3f"
      % (len(y_m), y_m.sum(), y_m.mean()))
print("evaluation set (random decoys) : %d molecules, %d actives, prevalence %.3f"
      % (len(y_r), y_r.sum(), y_r.mean()))
print(S_m.describe().round(3).to_string())

Figure 3. The four scores have completely different shapes. The two similarity scores are concentrated near 0.15-0.25 for decoys with a red tail of analogues stretching to 1.0; the random-forest probability is bimodal, pushed towards 0 and 1 by the trees; the descriptor distance is a smooth unimodal score with heavy overlap. Shapes matter for consensus - averaging raw scores of such different scales is meaningless, which is why section 13 standardises or ranks them first - and they matter for thresholding, because only the random-forest score carries anything resembling a probability.

4. The ROC curve and its area, from first principles

Sort the evaluation set by decreasing score and walk down the list. At every position, count how many actives have been seen (the true-positive rate, TPR: actives above the cut divided by all actives) and how many decoys have been seen (the false-positive rate, FPR). Plotting TPR against FPR as the cut slides from the top of the list to the bottom traces the receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) curve[27]. A useless ranking produces the diagonal; a perfect one rises to the top-left corner.

The area under that curve (ROC-AUC) has a probabilistic meaning worth memorising: it is the probability that a randomly chosen active is ranked above a randomly chosen decoy. That interpretation also gives the cheapest way to compute it, the Mann-Whitney statistic

$$\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{actives}} r_i - n_1 (n_1 + 1)/2}{n_1 n_0},$$

where $r_i$ is the rank of active $i$ when scores are sorted in increasing order, $n_1$ is the number of actives and $n_0$ the number of decoys. The next cell implements the curve and the formula, and checks both against scikit-learn.

def roc_curve_manual(y, s):
    '''TPR and FPR at every cut of the score-sorted list (ties broken by order, as in a real purchase list).'''
    o = np.argsort(-np.asarray(s), kind="mergesort"); ys = np.asarray(y)[o]
    tp = np.cumsum(ys); fp = np.cumsum(1 - ys)
    return np.r_[0, fp / fp[-1]], np.r_[0, tp / tp[-1]]

def roc_auc(y, s):
    '''Mann-Whitney form of the area under the ROC curve (average ranks handle ties).'''
    y = np.asarray(y); r = rankdata(s)
    n1 = y.sum(); n0 = len(y) - n1
    return (r[y == 1].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
print("max_tanimoto  ours %.6f | sklearn %.6f" % (roc_auc(y_m, S_m["max_tanimoto"]),
                                                  roc_auc_score(y_m, S_m["max_tanimoto"])))

5. Enrichment factors - and the ceiling nobody mentions

The enrichment factor at a fraction $f$ of the library is the most quoted number in the screening literature:

$$\mathrm{EF}_f = \frac{\text{actives found in the top } f}{\text{compounds in the top } f} \Big/ \frac{n_1}{N},$$

the hit rate in the top $f$ divided by the hit rate of the whole library. EF = 1 means the ranking is worthless; EF = 10 means the top of the list is ten times richer in actives than the library as a whole.

What is rarely said is that EF has a hard ceiling. If the top $fN$ positions are all actives, the hit rate there is 1 and $\mathrm{EF}_f = N / n_1 = 1/\text{prevalence}$. With this benchmark's prevalence of about 0.16, no ranking can score above about 6.2 at any fraction - and if $f$ is smaller than the prevalence, a perfect ranking fills the entire top fraction with actives and attains that ceiling exactly. Three of our four rankings do so at 1 %, which makes the metric useless for comparing them.

def enrichment_factor(y, s, frac):
    y = np.asarray(y); n = len(y); k = max(1, int(round(frac * n)))
    top = y[np.argsort(-np.asarray(s), kind="mergesort")][:k]
    return (top.mean()) / y.mean()

rows = []
for c in S_m.columns:
    rows.append(dict(ranking=c, AUC=roc_auc(y_m, S_m[c]),
                     EF1=enrichment_factor(y_m, S_m[c], 0.01),
                     EF5=enrichment_factor(y_m, S_m[c], 0.05),
                     EF20=enrichment_factor(y_m, S_m[c], 0.20)))
ef_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("ranking").round(3)
print("EF ceiling at this prevalence = 1/%.4f = %.3f" % (y_m.mean(), 1 / y_m.mean()))
print(ef_tab.to_string())

6. BEDROC and RIE: putting the weight where the money is

Truchon and Bayly proposed a metric that formalises the "early recognition" preference[1]. Give the active at relative rank $x = r/N$ an exponentially decaying weight $e^{-\alpha x}$, so that an active at the very top counts fully and one halfway down the list counts for almost nothing. The robust initial enhancement is the sum of those weights divided by its expectation under a random ranking,

$$\mathrm{RIE} = \frac{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i \in \text{actives}} e^{-\alpha r_i / N}} {\frac{1}{N}\,\frac{1 - e^{-\alpha}}{e^{\alpha/N} - 1}},$$

and BEDROC is RIE rescaled to the interval $[0, 1]$ so that 0 is the worst and 1 the best achievable ranking at the given prevalence $R_a = n_1/N$:

$$\mathrm{BEDROC} = \mathrm{RIE}\cdot\frac{R_a \sinh(\alpha/2)}{\cosh(\alpha/2) - \cosh(\alpha/2 - \alpha R_a)} + \frac{1}{1 - e^{\alpha(1 - R_a)}}.$$

The constant $\alpha$ sets how early "early" is: the weight falls to $1/e$ at $x = 1/\alpha$ and about 80 % of it lies in the top $4/\alpha$ of the list, so the conventional $\alpha = 20$ concentrates on the top 20 % and $\alpha = 160$ on the top few per mille. Choosing $\alpha$ after seeing the results is a form of multiple testing; fix it from the size of the campaign (test 50 of 10,000 compounds, $f = 0.005$, $\alpha \approx 4/f = 800$), accepting that so few actives in the top make the estimate noisy.

def rie_bedroc(y, s, alpha=20.0):
    '''Robust initial enhancement and BEDROC (Truchon & Bayly 2007), implemented from the definitions.'''
    y = np.asarray(y); ys = y[np.argsort(-np.asarray(s), kind="mergesort")]
    N = len(ys); n1 = int(ys.sum()); Ra = n1 / N
    r = np.where(ys == 1)[0] + 1.0
    rie = (np.exp(-alpha * r / N).sum() / n1) / ((1 / N) * (1 - np.exp(-alpha)) / (np.exp(alpha / N) - 1))
    scale = Ra * np.sinh(alpha / 2) / (np.cosh(alpha / 2) - np.cosh(alpha / 2 - alpha * Ra))
    return rie, rie * scale + 1 / (1 - np.exp(alpha * (1 - Ra)))

perfect = np.linspace(1, 0, len(y_m)) * 0 + y_m          # actives first
rand_s = np.random.default_rng(0).random(len(y_m))
print("sanity: perfect ranking BEDROC %.3f | random ranking BEDROC %.3f (prevalence %.3f)"
      % (rie_bedroc(y_m, perfect + np.linspace(0, 1e-6, len(y_m)))[1], rie_bedroc(y_m, rand_s)[1], y_m.mean()))

7. Hit rate at k: the number a medicinal chemist asks for

The metrics so far are dimensionless. The question actually asked in a project meeting is different: if I buy the top k compounds, how many will work? That is the hit rate at k, the fraction of actives among the first k entries, and its practical companion, the expected number of hits $k \times \text{hit rate}$. It depends on the prevalence of the evaluation set, which is precisely why it is the honest metric to carry into section 12.

8. Confidence intervals: how much of this is luck?

Every number printed so far is an estimate from one finite sample of actives and one finite sample of decoys. Replace the sample and the number moves. The standard way to quantify that movement without any distributional assumption is the bootstrap[28]: resample the data with replacement many times, recompute the statistic each time, and read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution as a 95 % interval.

For a screening benchmark the resampling must be stratified: draw $n_1$ actives with replacement from the actives and $n_0$ decoys with replacement from the decoys, so that every replicate has the same composition as the original and the prevalence - on which EF and BEDROC depend - is held fixed. Resampling the pooled list instead would make the prevalence fluctuate and mix two sources of variation. Note what this interval does and does not cover: it covers the sampling of molecules, not the choice of decoy set, not the choice of fingerprint, and not the choice of reference actives. Sections 9 to 11 measure those separately, and they are larger.

def bootstrap_ci(y, s, stat, n_boot=400, seed=0):
    '''Stratified bootstrap over actives and decoys; returns mean and a 95 % percentile interval.'''
    rg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ai, di = np.where(y == 1)[0], np.where(y == 0)[0]
    vals = np.empty(n_boot)
    for b in range(n_boot):
        idx = np.concatenate([rg.choice(ai, ai.size, True), rg.choice(di, di.size, True)])
        vals[b] = stat(y[idx], s[idx])
    return vals.mean(), np.percentile(vals, 2.5), np.percentile(vals, 97.5)

    a = bootstrap_ci(y_m, s, roc_auc)

    e = bootstrap_ci(y_m, s, lambda yy, ss: enrichment_factor(yy, ss, 0.20))
    ci_rows.append(dict(ranking=c, AUC="%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]" % a, BEDROC20="%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]" % b,
                        EF20="%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]" % e, auc_lo=a[1], auc_hi=a[2], auc_m=a[0]))

9. How many actives do you know? The reference set decides the score

The maximum-Tanimoto ranking used 530 training actives. A real project at its start knows five, or twenty, or - after a literature review of a well-studied target - a few hundred. Because the score of a candidate is the similarity to its closest known active, the number and the identity of those references are not a detail of the protocol: they are the protocol. The next cell repeats the same ranking with reference sets of 5 to 530 actives, ten random draws each, and reports the mean and the spread of the resulting AUC.

This also settles a comparison worth making. The frozen library's own README reports ROC-AUC 0.917 against matched decoys for a twenty-five-reference Tanimoto ranking; our ten draws of twenty-five references average 0.918, with individual draws from 0.827 to 0.945. The agreement of the means is reassuring, and the width of the band is the real message: a single draw of a reference set can land a tenth of an AUC unit away from the protocol's expectation. The enrichment factors, by contrast, reproduce the README exactly (6.21 against matched decoys, 3.84 against random ones) because both sit on the ceiling 1/prevalence and have nothing left to vary.

Figure 10. The same four rankings evaluated against property-matched decoys (left) and random decoys (right). The similarity rankings are almost unaffected (0.994 to 0.996), the QSAR random forest gains 0.037 AUC (0.960 to 0.997) and the descriptor distance gains 0.102 (0.856 to 0.958). The ordering of the methods changes: against random decoys the property-based random forest becomes the best in the panel, against matched decoys it is third.

That asymmetry is the argument for property matching[2][15]: a property-based score is rewarded by any decoy set whose properties differ from the actives, because the task it actually solves is "does this look like a kinase inhibitor?" rather than "does it bind ROCK1?". Substructure similarity is comparatively immune, the exclusion rule having already removed decoys close to known ligands. The laboratory rule: report every metric against the hardest decoy set you can build, and never compare methods evaluated against different decoys[12][14]. Matching is itself imperfect - decoys matched too tightly become near-actives and punish a method for finding them[16] - so benchmarks built from experimentally confirmed inactives (MUV[19], LIT-PCBA[18]) are now preferred, at the price of smaller and noisier active sets.

11. The artificial-enrichment diagnostic

There is a direct test of how much of a benchmark's separability lives in the properties rather than in the pharmacology: train a classifier that is only allowed to see the physico-chemical descriptors, with no fingerprint and no target information, and ask how well it distinguishes actives from decoys under honest cross-validation. If that classifier succeeds, any method using the same descriptors can succeed for the same uninteresting reason[3][17].

    sc = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                         X[sel], lab[sel], cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), scoring="roc_auc")
    diag[ds] = (sc.mean(), sc.std())

The diagnostic returns a 5-fold ROC-AUC of 0.983 against the matched decoys and 1.000 against the random ones. Read that carefully: a model that knows nothing but twelve bulk properties reproduces, and exceeds, the performance of every ligand-based ranking in section 3. The benchmark is therefore not measuring pharmacology; at best it measures the ability to recognise the chemical class from which ROCK1 inhibitors were drawn. This does not make the benchmark useless - relative comparisons between methods on the same decoys remain informative - but it forbids the sentence "our model achieves AUC 0.98 and has therefore learnt the binding determinants of ROCK1".

Three defences, all used by the group: report the diagnostic alongside the results as a declared property of the benchmark; prefer splits that break the property shortcut (a scaffold split, Unit 12) or decoys matched on more properties; and validate prospectively, the only evaluation no benchmark artefact survives.

Exercise 3

Remove FractionCSP3, QED and AromaticRings from PROPS and rerun the diagnostic. How far does the property-only AUC against the matched decoys fall? Then add Morgan fingerprint bits as features and rerun once more. Which of the three feature sets would you use to argue that a model has learnt something target-specific, and what would you still not be able to claim?

12. Prevalence, base rates and what the top of the list is really worth

The benchmark's active fraction is 16 % in the evaluation set. A purchasable screening library contains perhaps one active per thousand molecules for a tractable target, and far fewer for a hard one[30]. Prevalence does not affect ROC-AUC - the probability that an active outranks a decoy is unchanged if we delete nine out of ten actives at random - but it changes everything a project actually cares about.

12.1 The calculation by hand

Let the library contain $N$ compounds of which a fraction $\pi$ are active, and suppose our ranking puts a fraction $e$ of the actives into the top $f$ of the list. The hit rate among the compounds we buy is

$$\text{hit rate} = \frac{\pi e N}{f N} = \pi \cdot \frac{e}{f} = \pi \cdot \mathrm{EF}_f .$$

With $\pi = 0.001$ and an enrichment factor of 95 in the top 1 %, the hit rate is $0.001 \times 95 = 0.095$: about one compound in ten of the top 1 % is active. Buying fifty compounds from that top 1 % gives an expected $50 \times 0.095 = 4.8$ hits, against $50 \times 0.001 = 0.05$ for a random draw - a spectacular improvement that still means forty-five failures. Written as a posterior probability (the Bayes rule of Unit 10), the probability that a specific top-ranked compound is active is

$$P(\text{active}\mid\text{top } f) = \frac{P(\text{top } f\mid\text{active})\,\pi}{P(\text{top } f)} = \frac{e\,\pi}{f} = 0.095 ,$$

with $e = 0.95$ and $f = 0.01$. The next cell performs the experiment that this arithmetic predicts: it keeps the decoys fixed and subsamples the actives down to prevalences of 5 %, 1 % and 0.1 %, repeating each subsample 200 times.

def prevalence_experiment(S, y, col, prevalences=(0.161, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001), n_rep=200, seed=0):
    rg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = S[col].to_numpy(); ai, di = np.where(y == 1)[0], np.where(y == 0)[0]
    out = []
    for p in prevalences:
        n_a = min(len(ai), max(1, int(round(p * len(di) / (1 - p)))))
        ef1 = []; ef5 = []; auc = []; hr100 = []
        for _ in range(n_rep):
            idx = np.concatenate([rg.choice(ai, n_a, replace=False), di])
            yy, ss = y[idx], s[idx]
            ef1.append(enrichment_factor(yy, ss, 0.01)); ef5.append(enrichment_factor(yy, ss, 0.05))
            auc.append(roc_auc(yy, ss)); hr100.append(yy[np.argsort(-ss, kind="mergesort")][:100].mean())
        out.append(dict(prevalence=n_a / (n_a + len(di)), n_actives=n_a, AUC=np.mean(auc),
                        EF1=np.mean(ef1), EF1_ceiling=min(1 / (n_a / (n_a + len(di))), 100),
                        EF5=np.mean(ef5), hit_rate_top100=np.mean(hr100),
                        expected_hits_in_50=50 * np.mean(hr100)))
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

prev_tab = prevalence_experiment(S_m, y_m, "max_tanimoto").round(4)
print(prev_tab.to_string(index=False))

13. Consensus and rank aggregation: does combining help?

When several scores are available the reflex is to combine them. Four schemes are standard[5]:

  1. z-score consensus: standardise each score to mean 0 and unit variance, then average. Keeps magnitude information; sensitive to the shape of each score distribution.
  2. rank-by-rank: replace each score by its rank and average the ranks. Scale-free, insensitive to outliers, discards magnitude.
  3. rank-by-vote: count in how many rankings a compound appears in the top 5 %. Very robust, extremely coarse - most compounds get 0 votes, and ties are resolved arbitrarily.
  4. exponential consensus ranking (ECR): sum $e^{-r/\sigma}$ over the rankings, with $\sigma$ the number of hits one is willing to inspect (here 5 % of the list); it weights each ranking's top and ignores its tail.

Consensus helps when the rankings are comparably good and make uncorrelated errors, and hurts when a weak ranking votes with the same weight as a strong one. Our panel contains one excellent and one poor ranking, so the experiment below tests that principle rather than demonstrating that consensus works.

print("Spearman correlation between the four rankings (matched-decoy evaluation set):")
print(S_m.corr(method="spearman").round(2).to_string())

def consensus_scores(S, top_frac=0.05):
    Z = (S - S.mean()) / S.std()
    R = S.apply(lambda c: rankdata(-c))             # rank 1 = best
    sigma = top_frac * len(S)
    return pd.DataFrame({"cons_z": Z.mean(axis=1),
                         "cons_rank": -R.mean(axis=1),
                         "cons_vote": (R <= top_frac * len(S)).sum(axis=1),
                         "cons_ecr": np.exp(-R / sigma).sum(axis=1)}, index=S.index)

C_m = consensus_scores(S_m)
all_sc = pd.concat([S_m, C_m], axis=1)
cons_tab = pd.DataFrame({c: dict(AUC=roc_auc(y_m, all_sc[c]), BEDROC20=rie_bedroc(y_m, all_sc[c], 20)[1],
                                 EF20=enrichment_factor(y_m, all_sc[c], 0.20)) for c in all_sc.columns}).T.round(3)
print(cons_tab.to_string())

def paired_bootstrap_delta(y, s1, s2, stat=roc_auc, n_boot=400, seed=1):
    '''Difference stat(s1) - stat(s2) resampled on the SAME bootstrap replicates (paired).'''
    rg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ai, di = np.where(y == 1)[0], np.where(y == 0)[0]
    d = np.empty(n_boot)
    for b in range(n_boot):
        idx = np.concatenate([rg.choice(ai, ai.size, True), rg.choice(di, di.size, True)])
        d[b] = stat(y[idx], s1[idx]) - stat(y[idx], s2[idx])
    return d.mean(), np.percentile(d, 2.5), np.percentile(d, 97.5), float((d <= 0).mean())

    print("  %-10s %+.4f [%+.4f, %+.4f]  P(delta <= 0) = %.3f" % (c, m, lo, hi, p))

The z-score consensus loses 0.005 AUC, rank-by-rank 0.007, ECR 0.007 and rank-by-vote 0.207; in every case the paired bootstrap interval of the difference excludes zero, so these are small but real losses, not noise. Consensus is a variance-reduction device, not a free improvement: it pays when components are of similar quality with different failure modes - typically several docking functions on the same poses - and costs when one component is clearly better, which is when the temptation to combine everything is strongest. A paired bootstrap of the metric difference, not two separately reported numbers, is the minimum evidence a consensus claim needs[4].

14. Score-size correlation and ligand efficiency

Screening scores are often correlated with molecular size: bigger molecules make more contacts, so additive scoring functions reward them, and the top of a docking list fills with heavy, greasy compounds that are poor starting points for medicinal chemistry[29]. The remedy is a size-normalised score - ligand efficiency, the free energy of binding per heavy atom, $\mathrm{LE} = 1.37 \times \mathrm{pActivity} / N_{\text{heavy}}$ in kcal mol-1 per atom[8]. The diagnostic comes first: measure the correlation before correcting for it.

15. Building the list the laboratory will actually buy

The campaign ends with a decision: which fifty compounds. Three criteria compete. Score says take the top fifty. Diversity says that fifty analogues of one scaffold test one hypothesis fifty times, so spread the selection over chemotypes. Tractability says remove compounds with known assay-interference substructures (PAINS filters[33]), implausible properties or impossible chemistry. We implement the first two at a realistic 1 % prevalence and measure the trade-off; the third is a filter whose cost in hits should be measured the same way.

def select_lists(seed, n_pick=50, sim_cut=0.6, pool=500):
    '''Top-n and diversity-filtered top-n from a 1 %-prevalence version of the evaluation set.'''
    rg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ai, di = np.where(y_m == 1)[0], np.where(y_m == 0)[0]
    n_a = int(round(0.01 * len(di) / 0.99))
    idx = np.concatenate([rg.choice(ai, n_a, replace=False), di])
    yy, ss = y_m[idx], S_m["max_tanimoto"].to_numpy()[idx]
    o = np.argsort(-ss, kind="mergesort")
    top = o[:n_pick]
    chosen = [o[0]]
    for j in o[1:pool]:
        if len(chosen) == n_pick:
            break
        if max(DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[ev_m[idx[j]]], [fps[ev_m[idx[k]]] for k in chosen])) < sim_cut:
            chosen.append(j)
    chosen = np.array(chosen)
    sc = lib["scaffold_smiles"].to_numpy()[ev_m]
    return (yy[top].sum(), yy[chosen].sum(), len(set(sc[idx[top]])), len(set(sc[idx[chosen]])), n_a + len(di))

res = np.array([select_lists(s)[:4] for s in range(50)], dtype=float)
n_total = select_lists(0)[4]
print("library of %d compounds at 1 %% prevalence; 50 compounds purchased, 50 independent simulations" % n_total)

print("diverse-50 (T < 0.6) : %.1f +/- %.1f hits, %.1f distinct scaffolds" % (res[:, 1].mean(), res[:, 1].std(), res[:, 3].mean()))
print("random 50            : %.2f hits expected" % (50 * 0.01))

The fifty best-scoring compounds return 40.5 +/- 1.2 confirmed actives over 42.4 scaffolds; a Tanimoto < 0.6 dissimilarity filter applied while walking down the list returns 34.6 +/- 2.2 actives over 45.8 scaffolds - six hits traded for about three chemotypes, both far above the 0.5 hits of a random fifty.

Whether the trade is worth making is a project decision. To confirm a series, buy the top of the list; to find a new chemotype - the usual reason for screening - the diversity filter is cheap insurance. Report both numbers, expected hits and expected distinct scaffolds, each with its spread over simulations.

16. What a prospective campaign commits to

Every number in this notebook is retrospective: the labels existed before the ranking was built. A prospective campaign commits to a protocol in advance and is judged by the assay. The group's checklist, which doubles as the summary of this unit, is to state in writing before any compound is ordered: the library and its assumed active fraction; the ranking method with its reference set frozen; the metric and the $\alpha$ or fraction $f$ it uses; the number of compounds that will be bought; the diversity and filtering rules; the expected number of hits computed as $k \times \pi \times \mathrm{EF}$; and what result would count as a failure. Published prospective campaigns at very large scale[9][32] report hit rates of a few per cent from libraries of hundreds of millions of molecules - orders of magnitude better than random, and still a large majority of inactive purchases.

Benchmark numbers remain useful for relative decisions - which ranking to trust, how many references to collect, whether consensus earns its pipeline - but they are not predictions. Doing the prevalence arithmetic of section 12 in front of the collaborators, before the money is spent, is what separates a screening report from a screening advertisement[7].

17. Summary

A virtual screen delivers an ordering, and the analytics of that ordering are a self-contained data-science problem. This unit built four ligand-based rankings of the same 12,018-molecule library from training information only and measured them from first principles. ROC-AUC, implemented as the Mann-Whitney statistic, agrees with scikit-learn to six decimals and places maximum Tanimoto similarity (0.994) and the five-nearest-neighbour score (0.993) above a property-based random forest (0.960) and a descriptor distance (0.856). Enrichment factors at 1 % and 5 % were unusable here because they sit on their ceiling 1/prevalence = 6.21; at 20 % they separate the methods again. BEDROC and RIE weight the purchasable top at the price of a parameter alpha fixed in advance. Stratified bootstrap intervals are narrow here (0.994 [0.990, 0.997] for the best ranking) and would be several times wider on a typical in-house benchmark with fifty actives instead of 797.

The three honest lessons are larger than any of those numbers. First, the benchmark decides the answer: replacing property-matched decoys by random ones lifts the random forest from 0.960 to 0.997 and the descriptor distance from 0.856 to 0.958 while barely touching the similarity rankings, and the number of known actives used as references moves the same algorithm from 0.830 to 0.994, with draws of twenty-five references spanning 0.83 to 0.95. Second, a random forest that sees only twelve bulk properties separates actives from matched decoys at 5-fold AUC 0.983 and from random decoys at 1.000, so this benchmark cannot support any claim about learnt pharmacology - the artificial-enrichment diagnostic must be reported with the results. Third, the 16 % active fraction of the evaluation set is a fiction: at a realistic 0.1 % the same ranking still has AUC 0.996 and EF1% = 95, but the hit rate among the top hundred falls to 3.8 %, i.e. about two hits per fifty compounds purchased. Consensus did not rescue anything - all four aggregation schemes lost significantly to the best single ranking, because two of the four components were weak and the two strong ones were redundant (Spearman 0.96). Size normalisation was equally unnecessary: the similarity scores have no size bias to correct (rho = 0.00), and imposing ligand efficiency on them costs 0.006 AUC. Finally, a diversity filter at Tanimoto 0.6 traded about six hits for about three extra scaffolds in a fifty-compound purchase simulated at 1 % prevalence - the kind of trade that should be decided by the aim of the campaign and reported as two numbers, not one.

Three habits carry over. Report the composition of any benchmark (prevalence, decoy provenance, reference set) next to every metric it produced; use a paired test on the same resamples when comparing rankings; and convert retrospective enrichment into prospective expectation before promising anything to a collaborator. Diversity selection connects to the clustering of Unit 15 (Butina's leader algorithm[21] solves the same task), and the activity cliff[22] - a tiny structural change abolishing activity - is why no similarity ranking is ever more than a prior.

18. Self-assessment

1. A colleague reports "ROC-AUC 0.95" for a new ligand-based method. Which three pieces of information do you ask for before believing that it is better than maximum Tanimoto similarity?

The decoy set (provenance and whether it is property-matched), the reference set of known actives (how many, and whether it is the same one the baseline used), and the evaluation protocol (hold-out or cross-validation, and whether the baseline was run on exactly the same evaluation molecules). Section 9 showed a 0.16 AUC swing from the size of the reference set and a 0.12 spread across draws of the same size, and section 10 a 0.10 swing from the decoy set.

2. Why did three of the four rankings produce exactly the same EF at 1 % and 5 % in section 5?

Because the enrichment factor is capped at 1/prevalence, and with 16 % actives any ranking whose top 1 % and top 5 % contain only actives attains that cap, 6.21. The metric has no resolution left. Either evaluate at a fraction well above the prevalence, or subsample to a realistic prevalence, or use BEDROC.

3. What exactly does the parameter alpha of BEDROC control, and how should it be chosen?

It sets the exponential decay of the weight given to an active at relative rank x, e^(-alpha x); about 80 % of the weight lies in the top 4/alpha of the list. Choose it before the analysis from the size of the campaign: if you will test a fraction f of the library, alpha near 4/f weights the region you can afford. Choosing alpha after seeing the curves turns the metric into a selection effect.

4. A property-only random forest separates your actives from your decoys at AUC 0.98. What does that invalidate, and what does it not?

It invalidates any claim that performance on this benchmark demonstrates target-specific learning, because a model with no structural information achieves the same. It does not invalidate relative comparisons between methods evaluated on the identical decoy set, nor does it mean the ranking will fail prospectively - it means the benchmark cannot tell you whether it will.

5. Your screen has AUC 0.97 and EF at 1 % equal to 95 on a library with one active per thousand compounds. You will buy 50 compounds from the top 1 %. How many hits do you expect, and what is the probability that any given purchased compound is active?

Hit rate = prevalence x EF = 0.001 x 95 = 0.095, so about 4.8 hits in 50 purchases and a 9.5 % probability per compound. Against a random draw (0.05 hits) that is a factor of 95, and it still means roughly 45 inactive purchases.

6. Why must the bootstrap used for a screening metric resample actives and decoys separately?

Because EF, BEDROC and hit rate all depend on the prevalence of the evaluation set. Resampling the pooled list lets the number of actives fluctuate, mixing uncertainty about the metric with uncertainty about the benchmark composition, and inflating the interval. Stratified resampling holds the composition fixed, which is the quantity being studied.

7. Under what conditions does consensus scoring help, and how would you demonstrate that it helped?

When the component rankings are of comparable quality and make uncorrelated errors. Demonstrate it with a paired bootstrap of the metric difference on the same resamples, reporting the interval of the difference; two separately quoted AUCs are not evidence. In this unit all four schemes lost to the best single ranking, with intervals excluding zero.

8. A docking campaign returns a top list dominated by molecules of 45-55 heavy atoms. What do you check, and what do you do?

Check the Spearman correlation between score and heavy-atom count, and the AUC of ranking by size alone. If both indicate a size effect, re-rank by a size-normalised score (ligand efficiency) or stratify the selection by size bin, and report both lists. Do not apply the normalisation when the diagnostic is negative, as it was for the similarity scores here, because it destroys information.

9. Why is a diversity-filtered selection usually preferred over the raw top of the list, even though it buys fewer hits?

Because the purpose of most screens is to find a new chemotype, and fifty analogues of a single scaffold test one chemical hypothesis fifty times. The simulation in section 15 quantified the price: about six hits for about four additional scaffolds. Report both numbers and let the project aim decide.

10. Which parts of a retrospective evaluation does a bootstrap confidence interval NOT cover?

Everything that is a design choice rather than a sample: the decoy set, the reference actives, the fingerprint and similarity measure, the descriptor list, the model's hyperparameters and the metric's alpha. Those are quantified by re-running the analysis under alternative choices, as in sections 9 to 11, and their effect here was an order of magnitude larger than the sampling interval.

11. You are asked to write the prospective commitment for a fifty-compound campaign. List the items it must contain.

Library and assumed active fraction; ranking method with a frozen reference set; metric with its alpha or fraction f; number of compounds to be purchased; diversity and structural-alert filters; the expected number of hits computed as k x prevalence x EF; and the result that would count as a failure. All of it written before the order is placed.

12. The same method gives AUC 0.81 on your benchmark and 0.92 in the paper that proposed it. Name three mundane explanations before concluding that your implementation is wrong.

A different number or identity of reference actives (Figure 9: 0.83 to 0.95 across draws of 25); a different decoy set (Figure 10: up to 0.10 AUC); and a different evaluation subset or prevalence. Only after those are matched does a discrepancy point at the code.

Glossary

Active
A compound experimentally confirmed to act on the target above a stated potency threshold; here, ROCK1 inhibitors with pActivity at least 6.5.
Decoy
A molecule assumed inactive, added to a benchmark so that a ranking can be scored. Property-matched decoys resemble the actives in bulk properties; random decoys do not.
Prevalence (active fraction)
Proportion of actives in the evaluated set. Determines the ceiling of the enrichment factor and the hit rate of any purchase.
ROC curve / ROC-AUC
True-positive rate against false-positive rate along the ranked list; its area is the probability that a random active outranks a random decoy.
Enrichment factor (EF)
Hit rate in the top fraction f divided by the hit rate of the whole library; bounded above by 1/prevalence.
BEDROC / RIE
Early-recognition metrics that weight an active at relative rank x by exp(-alpha x); BEDROC is RIE rescaled to [0, 1] at the given prevalence.
Hit rate at k
Fraction of actives among the first k compounds of the ranking - the quantity a purchase decision is made on.
Artificial enrichment
Separability of actives from decoys that comes from benchmark construction (property differences) rather than from target pharmacology.
Analogue bias
Over-representation of close analogues among the actives, which inflates similarity-based metrics because one scaffold is found many times.
Tanimoto coefficient
Shared bits divided by the union of set bits of two fingerprints; the standard similarity for Morgan fingerprints.
Consensus / rank aggregation
Combining several rankings by averaging standardised scores, averaging ranks, counting votes or summing exponentially weighted ranks (ECR).
Ligand efficiency
1.37 x pActivity divided by the heavy-atom count: potency per atom, used to compare molecules of different size.
Scaffold (Bemis-Murcko)
The ring systems and their linkers after side chains are removed; the usual unit of chemical-series bookkeeping.
Prospective validation
Buying and testing compounds selected by a frozen protocol; the only evaluation immune to benchmark artefacts.
